newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Chun's death sentence commuted; families protest.
newsitem.headline: Chun's death sentence commuted; families protest.

text.p: The death sentence on former South Korean president Chun Doo Hwan was commuted to life imprisonment on Monday, sparking immediate outrage from families of victims of the 1980 Kwangju massacre that he ordered.

The Seoul High Court also cut to 17 years from 22-1/2 years the jail term for Chun's successor Roh Tae-woo. In an appeals hearing, judges also reduced jail terms of 12 former generals, kept one unchanged and upheld the acquittal of a 14th.

Chun and Roh were convicted in August of mutiny, treason and bribery over a 1979 coup that launched Chun's political career, the massacre of several hundred pro-democracy activists and their amassing hundreds of millions of dollars in slush funds.
Dressed in pale blue prison uniforms, the pair stood motionless side-by-side as the panel ruled on their conviction appeals in the country's so-called "Trial of the Century."
But the verdicts set off gasps of disbelief and anger within the courtroom, packed with 250 spectators including the families of some Kwangju massacre victims.
Outside the court, the mother of one victim, Lee Keum-soon, wept as she denounced the decision.

"This is unfair. This is obviously a prepared script. My son was handicapped during the Kwangju massacre. The people of Kwangju are still living with anger from that incident," the woman in her fifties told reporters.
Nearby, 15 protestors staged a sit-down demonstration.
"Bring back my son to life," one protester yelled.
The judges said Chun's sentence was commuted because of his help in the economic development of the now-booming Asian "Tiger' and the peaceful presidency transfer to Roh in 1988.
"Losing political power doesn't necessarily mean death," Chief Judge Kwon Sung said in delivering the verdict.
In reducing Roh's sentence the judge said:
"Although Roh is guilty of similar charges, we have to differentiate between a mastermind and a follower. So I give a 17 year prison sentence."
Chun has consistently denied ordering crack paratroopers to open fire on unarmed student demonstrators protesting against his grab for power in the 1979 putsch.
But he has defended his military crackdown as needed to quell civil insurrection that he said risked exposing capitalist South Korea to attack from communist North Korea.
Chun, president from 1980 to 1988, was fined 263 billion won ($311.6 million) and Roh, president from 1988 to 1993, was fined 226 billion won.
Both men patted each other encouragingly on the knee in the minutes leading up to the court's decision.
They sat awaiting their fate in light blue prison uniforms -- Chun as prisoner 3124 and Roh as prisoner 1042.
With them were the 14 ex-generals, most now white-haired who have risen to distinguished positions in civilian society.
Of 13 one-time commanders, the court reduced 12 of their sentences to between 3-1/2 and eight years from between four and 10 years. One sentence of seven years remained unchanged.
All defendants can make final appeals to the Supreme Court within the next seven days. President Kim Young-sam also can grant them pardons.
Later on Monday the High Court rules on appeals against bribery convictions by five businessmen and six former aides and bodyguards.
Kwangju families said the verdicts were a cynical political manipulation ahead of presidential elections next year.
Current head of state Kim Young-sam needs the support of rightwingers, who once rallied around Chun and Roh, in picking his successor after his single-term expires.
